li.a: CBS Texas: 2 dead, 3 injured, suspect arrested after two Carrollton shootings tied to business dispute, police say
CBS Texas: North Texas Korean community mourns victims, urges unity after K Towne Plaza shootings
FOX 4 Dallas-Fort Worth: Carrollton shooting suspect was tired of business associates 'taking his money,' report says
NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth: Two killed, three shot during business meeting in Texas
Associated Press, published by WDBJ: 2 killed and 3 injured in shootings near shopping mall, Texas police say
Associated Press, published by Spectrum News: Man accused in Dallas-area shootings charged with capital murder
ABC7 Chicago: Dallas-area shopping center shooting that left 2 dead, 3 injured was not random, officials say
Korea JoongAng Daily: 2 killed, 3 injured in Texas Koreatown shooting

content.p: On the morning of Tuesday 5 May 2026, police say a gunman opened fire in a Korean grocery inside K Towne Plaza, a shopping centre in the Koreatown district of Carrollton, Texas, on a group who were there to meet the man later charged. More than an hour later, police were called to a second killing, of a man in his apartment about four miles away. Two people were killed and three wounded. Police arrested a 69-year-old restaurant owner, Seung Ho Han, outside an H Mart supermarket, and on Wednesday said he faced a double capital murder charge, along with three assault charges involving a deadly weapon. Han is accused, not convicted, and no plea has been reported.

The case is notable less for its scale than for its setting and its cause. Carrollton is a city of about 130,000 people, 20 miles north of Dallas, and more than 4,000 of its residents are of Korean descent, according to the US Census Bureau figures cited by the Associated Press. Police statements and an arrest warrant affidavit describe a dispute over money between people who knew one another, not a random attack.
content.h2: A community built on small businesses
content.p: The Associated Press described Koreatown as an area that grew over about twenty years into a thriving centre for the Dallas metropolitan area, thanks to Korean investors. It is anchored by big stores such as the H Mart supermarket and holds dozens of restaurants and several Korean churches. K Towne Plaza, on State Highway 121 near Hebron Parkway, houses many Korean businesses, including the Gwangjang Korean Market.

The area worked like a small town. A woman whose mother owns a business in the area told NBC 5 that customers and retailers commonly know each other and that "it's kind of like a small town". Daniel Shin, who heads the Korean Chamber of Commerce North Texas, told CBS Texas he was acquainted with each victim and with the suspect, and that Han ran Kkanbu Sushi.

CBS Texas reported that Carrollton police and fire crews were sent to K Towne Plaza at 9:57 a.m. Officers found four adults with gunshot wounds, and one man was pronounced dead at the scene. The AP gave the time as just before 10 a.m. NBC 5 reported the call as having come at about 11 a.m., a different time from the other outlets, which put it before 10.

The wounded victims told detectives that they were at the shopping centre with Sung Rae Cho for a meeting when Han arrived and began shooting, according to the arrest warrant affidavit as reported by FOX 4. Police chief Roberto Arredondo said the meeting was a business matter. "We don't know exactly what the meeting was about, but we understand it to be a business relation," he told reporters on the day, according to ABC7.

As FOX 4 summarised the affidavit, Han arrived at the meeting and faced the group close to the store's entrance. It says he told them he did not have their rent but did have a pistol, collected their mobile phones and, after a very brief discussion, shot Young Yoo and the two Kims. It says he shot Cho as Cho ran toward the front exit. The medical examiner identified Cho as 63 years old and from Denton; CBS Texas reported that he died inside the market.

Investigators cordoned off a large part of the parking lot. Workers in nearby businesses told reporters they locked their doors when they learned of police activity. Julie Solis, who works near the plaza, told NBC 5 that her workplace locked down at once. Investigators set up a mobile command post in a McDonald's car park across the road, and the FBI was among the agencies collecting evidence in the parking lot, according to the AP.
content.h2: The second shooting and the arrest
content.p: While officers were still at the plaza, a call came in about a second shooting. CBS Texas gave the time as 11:13 a.m. and the place as the 2700 block of Old Denton Road, near I-35 and the George Bush Turnpike. Police found a second man dead in an apartment. The AP described the apartment complex as roughly four miles from the plaza. Officials identified him as Edward Schleigh, FOX 4 reported.

According to the affidavit as summarised by FOX 4, Han drove to Schleigh's apartment, having said he knew Schleigh never locked the door, and walked in. Han told detectives he said he was tired of Schleigh taking his money and shot him twice. FOX 4 also reported that Schleigh's attorney turned up and told detectives his client was in a business arrangement with the owners of the plaza that was the site of the first shooting.

Han was taken into custody outside the H Mart supermarket after a short foot chase. Witnesses told NBC 5 they saw officers put handcuffs on a man in a blue shirt in front of the store. Law enforcement had surrounded the supermarket, and a bomb squad and ATF personnel were seen at the cordon. Police used a robot to check a white van in the parking lot before towing it away, NBC 5 reported. According to the affidavit as quoted by FOX 4, Han said he had driven to the H Mart fish market to say goodbye to friends and planned to take his own life.

Carrollton police said that in an interview Han admitted to detectives that he was the gunman and gave his reason as anger over money disputes with the people he shot. CBS Texas reported that detectives said he confessed to shooting all five victims. FOX 4 reported that Han waived his rights before speaking.

The affidavit supplies the detail. FOX 4 reported that Han told detectives he felt exploited and wanted back more than $75,000. He named Yoo and Schleigh as his counterparts. In the affidavit's account Yoo was the plaza's owner, and Schleigh was the real estate agent who, in the affidavit's words, "had convinced Han to purchase the sushi restaurant in the K-Towne shopping center last summer."

The affidavit goes on to say that the two men persuaded Han to put money into a Georgia property: $70,000 to Schleigh and $5,000 to Yoo. Schleigh agreed to pay the rent on Han's business as part of that deal, but the agreement eventually fell through, the document says. Han said he asked for his money back and was refused. He also said that Olivia Kim persuaded Yoo to raise his rent by $2,000. These are Han's statements to police as recorded in a warrant affidavit. They are allegations and have not been tested in court.

Korean community leaders gave a similar outline. CBS Texas reported that the leaders described the quarrel as involving a property manager, an owner and listing agents, and they urged people not to spread misinformation. Shin said both of the dead men were longtime business owners who had helped build K Towne Plaza, and that one of the injured was the property owner.

Police did not release the victims' names on the first day. By 6 May the medical examiner had identified Sung Rae Cho, and FOX 4 reported that officials named Cho and Edward Schleigh as the dead. It named Olivia Kim, Yo Sung Kim and Young Yoo as the wounded, all expected to survive. Police said the three injured people were in stable condition.

Little has been made public about the dead beyond their ages, residences and business ties. Community leaders told CBS Texas that two of the victims belonged to the local Korean Chamber of Commerce and took part in its work. Shin said one of the wounded was still struggling in hospital and that he was praying for him.

On Wednesday 6 May, Korean leaders gathered at the Korean Cultural Center of Dallas to pay their respects. CBS Texas said wreaths bearing condolence messages stood in the centre and flowers were placed at an altar for the victims. Young Sung, a former Carrollton councilman and Chamber of Commerce board member, said he personally knew all of those involved. "It hurts," he said. He told the station that he had lived in the area for decades and that the violence had shocked the Korean community locally and abroad, coming from a country where guns are heavily restricted.

The Consulate of the Republic of Korea in Dallas called the incident "devastating and shocking" and asked people not to spread unverified rumours while the investigation continued. The cultural center said it planned to set up donation funds for the victims and their families.

The Korean Society of Dallas held a news conference the same morning. Its president, Sungchul Woo, went to see the scene himself. "They all worked hard, as immigrants," he told FOX 4, adding that they work for their families and look after each other. John Jun, who is active in the Korean American community, told the AP, "We're shocked," and added, "We're not immune to something like this happening, but we are very generally a peaceful community that works hard."
Of the accused, Shin said, "He was a good guy," and added, "I don't know why he did that way."

Han was held in Denton County Jail on 6 May. Jail records did not then list an attorney for him, the AP reported. Police said the investigation continued with help from the FBI and the Texas Department of Public Safety. It has not been reported whether a grand jury has indicted Han, what he has pleaded, whether prosecutors will seek the death penalty, or when any trial might be held.

Reports at the start gave the accused's name as Seung Han Ho, including in NBC 5 and ABC7 coverage and in remarks by the police chief. The Associated Press corrected the spelling to Seung Ho Han. One report, originally written in Korean, gave it as Han Seung-ho.
